meta.title: Store, share, and update client .env files in 1Password
meta.lead: Every client's environment file lives in one place: a Secure Note in that client's 1Password vault. If you remember one thing: never send a credential — point people at the vault, and send a private link if they need help finding it.
meta.frequency: A new project needing a .env.local file, or any change to a stored value
meta.duration: ~5 minutes for Phases 1–5; 30–45 minutes for Phase 6

items.d: Client website projects need configuration values — API keys, account IDs, secrets — to run. This puts the complete .env.local file for every client in one controlled place in 1Password, so credentials stop moving through chat, email and shared drives, and anyone picking up a project can get running without asking a teammate to send them a file.
Every client website project that needs a .env.local file to run locally, and the complete contents of that file — every variable in it, not a filtered subset.

Production deployment configuration, version control, and scheduled audits of stored files. This is about storing, sharing and updating the file in 1Password, and where each value comes from. Nothing else.

blocks.t: Four standing rules
blocks.d: These hold on every project. Everything else in this document is procedure; these are not per-project judgement calls.

items.t: The complete file goes in the note
items.d: Every variable in .env.local, comment lines included. A Secure Note is free-form text, so the file goes in exactly as it appears on disk — paste in, copy out, no reassembly and no filtering.

items.t: Update the date header on every change
items.d: Without exception. It is the only signal anyone has that their local copy is stale.
Post in the Web Team Google Chat group. Nothing propagates automatically.
No .env file and no individual key through chat, email or a shared drive. Point the person at the vault instead. A private link is a pointer, not a credential, and is fine to send — see task 5.4.

blocks.text: One Secure Note per client, stored inside that client's existing vault.

rows: The client's vault (for example Awayframes), or <Client> – Dev where the client vault is shared beyond the dev team

blocks.t: The prefix is deliberate
blocks.text: Searching ENV — in 1Password returns every environment file across every client vault in one view.

items.d: A plain text file at the project root holding configuration as NAME=value lines, one per line. Read by the site when it runs.
A 1Password item type that stores free-form text. Holds the full contents of a .env.local file.
Line 1 of every note, in the form # UPDATED YYYY-MM-DD — <name>. Records when the note last changed and who changed it.
A 1Password link that opens a specific item directly. Resolves only for people who already have access to that vault, so it points at a credential without revealing one.
A key pointing at the live client system. Handles real bookings and real money.
Private Integration Token. GoHighLevel's per-location API credential.
Conversions API. Meta's server-side event endpoint; its access token is a credential.
Supabase's highest-privilege key. Bypasses row-level security.

blocks.text: What are you trying to do?
Six procedures. They are independent — pick the one that matches your situation and go straight to it.

items.t: Get a file onto your machine
items.d: Tasks 1.1–1.9. New machine, new project, or someone just changed a value.
Tasks 2.1–2.8. A key was rotated or replaced at the service that issued it.
Tasks 3.1–3.8. The project needs a value that is not in the note yet.
Tasks 4.1–4.2. Someone new needs to run the project.

items.t: Send a link to the note
items.d: Tasks 5.1–5.5. Point someone who already has access straight at the item.
Tasks 6.1–6.5. Revoke, then rotate. Revoking alone is not enough.

blocks.text: Phase 1 — Get a file onto your machine
blocks.d: New machine, new project, or after someone updates a value.

blocks.t: Search 1Password for ENV — <Client>
blocks.d: The ENV — prefix narrows the search to environment files only, across every client vault.

blocks.t: Open the item ENV — <Client> (.env.local)
blocks.expect: A line beginning # UPDATED at the top of the note.

blocks.t: Read line 1 and confirm the date is not older than your last local copy

body.t: If the note has no date header
body.text: Do not use it. Ask in the Web Team Google Chat group who edited it last and have them add one.

blocks.t: Copy the entire note contents
blocks.d: Comment lines included. Do not select a subset of variables.

body.caption: The Secure Note open in 1Password, date header on line 1, note body showing NAME=value lines and comments.

blocks.t: Open the project folder in VS Code
Right-click the project root in the Explorer pane and select New File

body.caption: VS Code Explorer right-click menu with New File highlighted, at the project root.

blocks.t: Name the file .env.local and press Return

body.t: Create it in VS Code, not Finder
body.text: Finder hides dotfiles, so a file you create there will not show up afterward and you will make a second one.

blocks.t: Paste the copied contents into the file, then save with Cmd + S
Run the project locally
blocks.expect: The site builds and serves without a missing-environment-variable error.

blocks.d: A key was rotated or replaced at the service that issued it.

blocks.t: Obtain the new value from the service that issued it
Open ENV — <Client> (.env.local) in 1Password
Click Edit
Replace the value in place
blocks.d: Leave the variable name and any comment above it untouched.

blocks.t: Change line 1 to today's date and your name
Click Save

body.caption: The note in edit mode with the date header line selected.

blocks.t: Post the change in the Web Team Google Chat group
blocks.d: Nothing propagates automatically. This message is the entire mechanism.

body.text: ENV updated for <Client> — re-copy before your next local run.
body.label: POST THIS IN WEB TEAM CHAT

blocks.t: Update your own .env.local

blocks.d: The project needs a value that is not in the note yet.

blocks.t: Obtain the value from the service that issues it
Open ENV — <Client> (.env.local) in 1Password
Click Edit
Add a comment line stating what the variable is for and which service issues it
Add the variable below it as NAME=value, on its own line
Change line 1 to today's date and your name
Click Save
Post the addition in the Web Team Google Chat group

body.text: New variable added to ENV for <Client> — re-copy before your next local run.
body.label: POST THIS IN WEB TEAM CHAT

blocks.text: Phase 4 — Give someone access to a project
blocks.d: Someone new needs to run the project locally.

blocks.t: Ask Gillian or Kyle to add the person to the client's vault
blocks.d: In the Web Team Google Chat group. Where a <Client> – Dev vault exists, use that one.
blocks.expect: They appear in the vault's member list in 1Password.

blocks.t: Send them this SOP ID and tell them to follow Phase 1

body.text: Everything they need is in the vault once access is granted. Sending a value “just to unblock them” is the exact thing this SOP exists to stop.

blocks.text: Phase 5 — Send someone a direct link to the note
blocks.d: Use this when someone with vault access asks where the file is. A private link opens the item in their own 1Password app, so they do not have to search.

blocks.t: Confirm the person already has access to the client's vault
blocks.d: If they do not → run Phase 4 first. A private link will not work for them until they do.

blocks.t: Open ENV — <Client> (.env.local) in 1Password

body.t: The item must be in a shared vault
body.text: Private links do not resolve for items in a Private vault.

blocks.t: Click the ellipsis … on the item
blocks.d: Available in the desktop app, the browser extension, and on 1password.com.

blocks.t: Select Copy Private Link

body.caption: The item ellipsis menu open in 1Password with Copy Private Link highlighted, showing Share as a separate entry.

body.text: The same menu offers Share, which creates a link anyone can open without a 1Password account and which reveals the full contents of the note. Never use Share on an ENV note. Copy Private Link resolves only for people who already have vault access, which is why it is safe to paste into chat.

blocks.t: Paste the link into the Web Team Google Chat group, or into your reply to their request
blocks.expect: They open the link and land directly on the item in their own 1Password app.

blocks.d: Removing vault access does not revoke a credential the person already copied to their laptop. Rotation is required, not optional.

blocks.t: Ask Gillian or Kyle to remove the person from every client vault they held
List every project they had access to
blocks.d: Write the list down before you start rotating. Phase 6 is the one procedure where losing your place has real consequences.

blocks.t: Rotate every credential below, at the service that issued it
blocks.d: For each project on your list. Record each new value as you go.

rows: Stripe — regenerate after rotating the secret key
Generated per site — regenerate each one

blocks.t: Replace every rotated value in each affected note
blocks.d: Open the note, click Edit, paste each new value, then change line 1 to today's date and your name.
blocks.expect: Every affected note carries today's date on line 1.

blocks.t: Post completion in the Web Team Google Chat group, naming each project you rotated

body.text: Access removed for <name>. Rotated and updated ENV for: <project>, <project>.
body.label: POST THIS IN WEB TEAM CHAT

items.t: Every credential in the note is usable
items.d: Because the complete file is stored, a note may contain production credentials. Anyone with vault access can use them, and anyone who has already copied the file keeps them until they are rotated. Phase 6 is the only thing that closes that.

items.t: A client vault shared beyond the dev team
items.d: Create <Client> – Dev and store the note there instead. Do not put a .env note in a vault that people outside the dev team can open.

items.t: Someone outside the HGM 1Password account needs a value
items.d: A private link will not work for them. Do not use Share on the ENV note. Create a separate temporary item containing only the value they need, share that, then delete it.

items.t: Revisit this SOP ahead of its review date
items.d: If a stale local copy causes an incident or a repeated time loss; if a contractor joins who needs access cut off cleanly; or if more than four people need local access to the same project.

blocks.t: What this SOP does not protect against
blocks.text: Stated plainly so nobody assumes more than is true. Plaintext copies still exist on individual laptops — this stops files moving through chat and email, it does not eliminate local copies. Nobody is notified automatically when a value changes; standing rule 3 is the entire mechanism. And a credential someone has copied cannot be recalled — Phase 6 is the only way to close it.

rows: Site fails to start with a missing environment variable error
A variable was added to the note after you last copied it. Repeat Phase 1.
The note has no # UPDATED date header
Do not use it. Ask who edited it last and have them add one.
.env.local does not appear after you create it
You created it in Finder, which hides dotfiles. Delete it and repeat tasks 1.5–1.8.
No 1Password vault exists for a new client
Request the vault from Gillian or Kyle. Do not store the file anywhere else in the meantime.
Gillian or Kyle, Web Team Google Chat
A private link opens to an error or an empty item
Confirm you are signed in to the HGM account and have access to that client's vault.
Gillian or Kyle, Web Team Google Chat
A credential was sent through chat, email or a shared drive
Rotate it at the issuing service, update the note per Phase 2, then delete the message.
A value in the note does not work
Confirm you copied the whole note and did not truncate a long value. If it still fails, rotate at source and run Phase 2.

blocks.t: Escalation
blocks.text: Every row above escalates to the Web Team Google Chat group. Gillian (Operations Manager) and Kyle Zinger (Web & Content Specialist) are the 1Password admins and can act on any vault or access issue.
Phase 6 is the one flow here with a point of no return: until every credential is rotated, the person who left still holds working keys. Run this before you call it done.
